I went back to the <PLACE> and found the new wing still under construction,
a thing that has been said of many great buildings, but it was never
said of the <PERSON>, because it is so difficult to build a house when
it is not even finished. It had a vague air of something left over; it
seemed like the end of the world in its way. I stood outside, gazing at
the new building, and suddenly I saw, not for the first time in my life,
that the real purpose of art is to make men see the things they have
never seen before. It is true, indeed, that if all art were to cease
men would still see the sky. But we should not see the clouds. If all
art ceased I should still see the moon, but I should not know that it was
a moon. The moon is not a moon; it is a piece of silver, and it is only
art that turns it into a symbol. Art does not merely describe the sky;
it describes the sky by itself. It is not that it makes us see the sky,
but that it creates the idea of the sky. I do not mean to say that the
<PERSON> is better than any other building; it is not better; but it is
different. It is not that it is more like the sky; it is that it is the
sky.

samples.prompt: Write three short anecdotal examples illustrating how unconventional or eccentric behavior can be more persuasive than eloquent rhetoric.
samples.generated:
It is not necessary to go any further in this direction to show that the
greatest orators are not only not infallible, but often very fallible.
I remember an incident of this kind when I was a boy; it happened in a
very small town in <ORG>. The mayor came to the hall with a speech
which was to be read by a servant on his behalf. But the speech was
so bad and so ridiculous that the whole hall burst into laughter; and
the servant, after reading it, said: “I beg your pardon, gentlemen. It
is quite true that the town of <PLACE> is not particularly beautiful;
but then, gentlemen, if you were ever so good as to come and see it, you
would find that it is almost always dark, except at night.” The audience
was completely stunned; they could not help admitting that the speech was
more convincing than the most elaborate and elaborate and eloquent speech
of any great orator. Then one of the gentlemen in the audience, who had
had some experience in the matter, proposed that the mayor should read
his own speech; which he did in the most solemn style; and the effect
was precisely the same as before.

“Sir,” he began, “I wish to express my humble thanks to all
those who have contributed to this fund....” And it is safe to say
that there was no such effect, because it was not the thing said; it
was merely the thing heard. It is not difficult to imagine the effect,
because we hear it every day.
